analysis.summary:
No field in this group fell below 80% in the main pilot. But almost every scale is missing a rule, and coders only agreed because they read the validator or made the same guess. The written band edges overlap or leave gaps (speed at 1.0 and 1.5, cooldowns of 11-14 s). Range has two framings that contradict each other (the unit's other weapons vs the screen) and no anchor. Sight has no anchor and no rule for games without fog. Sensor traits mix sourced facts with proposals (the IFV sample's radar). Raw speed agreed only 63.9% in the speed test.

I propose:
- one convention for numeric edges that matches validate.mjs
- exact edges for speed and cooldown
- a range rule anchored on the game's basic rifle and the unit's own sight
- a sight rule anchored on the reference infantry, with two new reference fields in the registry
- a sensors basis that covers sight only, with traits never proposed
- a series-title convention and a speed_raw rounding rule
- a fix to the SC2 registry note and to the IFV sample
- small clarifications for tiers, price and resources

For decision 2C I recommend method A for every unit. It agreed more (100% vs 94%, though that gap is one judged vehicle). The main reason is that it keeps one scale per field, the same scale cards use. The cost: shooter vehicles bunch into fast and very fast, and PlanetSide 2 tracked tanks get flagged ATYPICAL. Three changes flip choices all coders agreed on, by design: the helicopter's proposed long sight becomes medium; the TV missile and the Siege Tank's siege gun become off-screen; the IFV's stun bark goes from long to short.

speed_decision.evidence:
Speed test: 12 vehicles from Battlefield 4, PlanetSide 2 and Foxhole, three coders. Agreement: method A 100% (all 12 items agree); method B 94.4% (11 of 12). The one split is the PS2 Sunderer, which has no figure (A medium, B slow, C medium). Raw speed agreed only 63.9%, from rounding of m/s values plus one helicopter figure in an unclear unit (C used Gamepressure's '160'). The 6-point gap rests on one judged vehicle, so it is weak evidence.

Spread across bands. Under A, 6 of 12 vehicles are very fast and all four PS2 vehicles share one band; Battlefield uses fast (Abrams, LAV) and very fast (ITV, Viper); Foxhole uses medium and very slow. Under B, 8 of 12 are medium; Battlefield uses medium, fast and very fast; PS2 still shares one band (medium); Foxhole matches A, because its tank is barely faster than a walking soldier.

Tracks. Under A the PS2 Prowler (2.82) and Lightning (2.99) are very fast, which the tracks mobility does not allow, so they would be flagged 'mobility:tracks allowed.speed-bands very-fast' (coder C noted this). Under B they are medium.

Aircraft. The Viper is very fast under both methods (14.1 and 8.25). B separates nothing in the air; all three coders said so.

The 1.0 edge. Under B every anchor tank (Abrams, Prowler, Silverhand) sits exactly on 1.0, which the written bands give to both slow and medium. All three coders flagged it.

Foxhole road vs off-road. The registry says to use off-road speeds. That makes the O'Brien armoured car (0.65 / 0.60) and the Dunne truck (0.69 / 0.64) very slow under both methods, slower than a walking soldier, and they would be flagged ATYPICAL against the wheels rule. On roads they are the fastest vehicles in the test (Dunne 3.46 under A).

Battlefield boost. Since Battlefield 3 the vehicle boost has no meter (Battlefield Wiki, as the coders read it). Leaving it out, as the task told them, is inconsistent with the unlimited sprint used for the soldier. With boost, the LAV-25 goes from fast to very fast under A; under B, mixing a boosted IFV with an unboosted tank gives fast instead of medium.

Walking vs sprint reference. Foxhole uses walking (5 m/s, because sprint drains stamina); Battlefield and PS2 use sprint (6.5 m/s). A Foxhole sprint reference would move the Silverhand from medium to slow under A.

Mixed scales under B. The field would hold two scales, so typed links such as speed:>=fast, and the generator, would compare a soldier-scale band with a tank-scale band (coder C).
speed_decision.recommendation:
Use method A for every unit, vehicles and aircraft included, with the rules in rule_text.

Why:
- It agreed more, though only by one judged vehicle.
- It keeps one scale per field, and that scale matches the cards: a Shamble soldier is 1.0. The generator and typed links then compare like with like.
- Nothing is lost. Method B can be recomputed whenever figures exist: divide the vehicle's speed_raw by the standard tank's speed_raw.

Costs to accept:
- In shooters and modern RTS games most vehicles land in fast or very fast. mobility.notes must therefore say how each vehicle compares with the game's standard tank (or, for aircraft, its standard transport helicopter).
- PS2, Wargame and Broken Arrow tanks will be flagged ATYPICAL against the tracks speed rule. Under decision 4B the mobility group may want to turn that rule into a rarity.
- Foxhole wheeled vehicles come out very slow off-road. I suggest keeping the off-road rule and giving the road speed in notes. If you would rather band wheeled vehicles by road speed, say so.

If you choose B instead, it needs four extra rules: a second anchor for aircraft (the game's standard transport helicopter); a flag on each unit saying which scale it uses, so links and the generator never mix scales; the edge rule (the anchor tank itself is medium); and the same boost and road rules as A.
speed_decision.rule_text:
data/vocab/speed-bands.json description: 'Speed as a ratio to a reference unit. For source units the reference is the game's basic rifle infantry, named in the games registry, and every unit of that game is compared with it, vehicles and aircraft included. For generated cards it is a Shamble Frontlines soldier. Compare the speeds each can keep up for as long as it likes: count a sprint or a boost only when nothing limits it (no meter, stamina or cooldown), for the reference and the unit alike. Use the stock unit with no upgrades, on the ground it normally fights on: land speed for land units, amphibious ones included; water speed for boats; off-road speed where a game gives road and off-road speeds. A ratio exactly on an edge goes to the band nearer medium: 0.7 is slow, 1 and 1.5 are medium, 2.5 is fast. The validator computes the band from speed_raw the same way. There is no band for standing still.'

Terms: very-slow 'Under 0.7 times the reference.'; slow 'From 0.7 up to but not including 1 times the reference.'; medium 'From 1 up to and including 1.5 times the reference. The reference unit itself is medium.'; fast 'Over 1.5 and up to and including 2.5 times the reference.'; very-fast 'Over 2.5 times the reference.'

schemas/source-unit.schema.json mobility.speed: 'Ratio to the game's speed reference, its basic rifle infantry, for every unit, vehicles and aircraft included (see Speed bands). Where most of the game's vehicles come out fast or very fast, say in mobility.notes how this unit compares with the game's standard tank, or for aircraft with its standard transport helicopter.'

proposals.evidence:
Speed test: raw speed agreed 63.9% (6 of 12 items), below the threshold.
- Rounding splits: Abrams 11.111 / 11.11 / 11.111; LAV 11.667 / 11.67; Prowler 18.333 / 18.33; Lightning 19.444 / 19.44.
- Viper: A and B 91.667 (the Battlefield 3 infobox's 330 km/h); C 44.444 (Gamepressure's Battlefield 4 figure of '160', in a game unit the guide says matches no real unit).
- ITV: B 20.83 (a Battlefield 3 figure from the German wiki, marked judged); A and C none.
- The 'judged' flag split on the Viper: B said true for a figure from another title, A and C said false.
Pilot units: 4 hesitations in 4 reports. A-, B- and C-battlefield asked which model's figure to use (AH-1Z at 330 or Mi-28 at 320 km/h) and which title, since Battlefield 4 gives none. B-coh1 asked whether to record 1.0 for the reference unit itself. Unclear-rule flags: A-battlefield, B-battlefield.
proposals.root_cause: The speed_raw description says only 'when a stat table gives it'. It has no rounding rule. It does not say which title of a series or which mirrored model supplies the figure, whether a figure in an unclear unit counts, or when a band counts as judged.
proposals.change: Replace the description with: 'The unit's speed divided by the speed reference's, both from sources and in the same unit of measure, rounded to two decimals at the end. Record it whenever the sources give both figures, the reference unit itself included (1). A figure whose unit of measure the source leaves unclear does not count. For a series game, take the figure as the Series games convention says, and name the title and model in mobility.notes. With no usable figure, leave it out: the band is then judged from words, and confidence says so. Stored only so the band can be recomputed; the generator and app never show or use it.'

Speed test:

proposals.change:

Edges are exact, and a value on an edge takes the higher band. An ability with no wait has no band: leave cooldown out. That covers instant orders such as unloading, and mode switches that only take time to finish; put the switch time in the summary. An ability held back only by a shared team stock, such as Company of Heroes munitions, has no band unless the source also gives a cooldown.'

proposals.change:
List description: 'How far a weapon reaches, relative to the top-down screen. For source units the band compares the weapon with its own game: with the reach of the game's basic rifle and with its own unit's sight (see each term's coding rule and the tie-breaks), not with the screen and not with the unit's other weapons. Each weapon gets one band, from its longest reach against any target.'

source_rule on each term:
- melee: 'Hits only at touching distance: claws, blades, a bite, or a leap or latch onto the target.'
- short: 'Longest reach under 0.7 times the reach of the game's basic rifle (registry range_reference).'
- medium: 'Longest reach from 0.7 up to and including 1.5 times the basic rifle. The basic rifle itself is medium.'
- long: 'Longest reach over 1.5 times the basic rifle, and not past the unit's own sight.'
- off-screen: 'Reaches past its own unit's sight: a range figure above the unit's own sight figure, or the source says it needs spotters or fires beyond its own view. Also any shot steered through its own camera, such as a TV-guided missile. A scope or zoom alone is not enough.'

tie_breaks:
- [long, off-screen]: 'Check off-screen first, and pick it only for the reasons in its coding rule. A weapon with a scope or zoom that does not reach past its unit's sight stays long.'
- [short, medium, long]: 'Use the longest reach against any target: a launcher that reaches twice as far against aircraft is banded by its air reach. Use the maximum reach, not where the weapon works best: "best at 10-20 m" is not a reach. With no figure, go in this order. If the source compares the reach with a named weapon that has a figure, take that weapon's band, and move one band up or down only when the source says much further or much shorter. If the source calls the weapon short-, medium- or long-ranged, or says it outranges most units (long), take that band. Otherwise take the family's default range. Words about distance alone never make a weapon off-screen.'
- [melee, short]: 'Melee only when the weapon touches its target. A weapon that crosses any gap, however small, is short or longer.'

weapon.range description, replace 'Relative to the source's other weapons.' with: 'One band per weapon, from its longest reach against any target, compared with the game's basic rifle and with the unit's own sight (see Range bands); not compared with this unit's other weapons.'

review.speed_decision_review:
I agree with method A for every unit. I checked the figures in research/pilot/round-1/speed: band_a 100% (12 of 12), band_b 94.4% (the only split is the PS2 Sunderer, which no coder had a figure for), raw 63.9% (m/s rounding plus C's unexplained '160'). The gap between methods rests on one judged vehicle, so it is not the argument. The argument is the one the analyst gives. A keeps one scale per field, and that scale matches cards and typed links (speed:>=fast in the raider and scout roles). B can always be recomputed from speed_raw. B would also need an air anchor, a scale flag on every unit and an edge rule for the anchor tank, and it still bunches PS2 and every aircraft.

The costs of A are real but deterministic. The ATYPICAL flags on PS2, Wargame and Broken Arrow tanks (tracks allow up to fast) and on Foxhole wheeled vehicles (off-road speed, while wheels allow medium and up) follow from the band, so they do not lower agreement. The mobility group should still decide under 4B whether those speed limits become rarities for source units. Also flag to the mobility group: if Battlefield's boost counts in the speed because it is unlimited, it should not also be recorded as a boost trait.

The rule_text needs these fixes before it goes in (see my speed-method-a revision):
- The reference is not always rifle infantry: supcom and pa use a basic bot, mechwarrior a medium mech.
- 'The ground it normally fights on' invites a creep reading for Zerg, against the r5 note that says base speed with no creep.
- Say 'empty' and 'full health': Foxhole uses the empty truck, Generals the healthy speed.
- Make the vehicle-to-vehicle note unconditional. A coder working one unit cannot know whether most of the game's vehicles are fast.
- The speed_raw rule's 'unit of measure unclear' clause would drop the unitless game values that most RTS ratios are built on.

Confirm the Vehicle Boost page (B cites it) before writing the Battlefield boost line. Keep Foxhole on off-road speeds, with road speed in notes.

verdicts.reason: What works: the helicopter comes out at 14.1 for A, B and C, C's Gamepressure '160' drops out, and storing ratios removes the m/s rounding splits. What breaks: 'a figure whose unit of measure the source leaves unclear does not count' hits most RTS games. The RA3 wiki's land speeds (Conscript 50, Hammer 75, IFV 120, Drone 150) are unitless game values. So are RA1/RA2, Generals, Tempest Rising, Iron Harvest, SupCom, PA, DoW, SC2's 3.15 and WiC's 0-100 score, and the registry builds every ratio from them. Read literally, the RA3, SC2 and CoH pilot units would lose speed_raw. The real test is whether both figures are on the same scale. Three smaller problems. (1) The reference figure comes from the registry, not from the unit's sources. (2) 'Confidence says so' points at a rating for the whole unit; a per-field doubt belongs in uncertain[]. (3) Rounding to two decimals can push a ratio across an edge (0.696 becomes 0.70, slow), so the text must say the band follows the stored value, as validate.mjs line 494 does.
verdicts.revised_change: Replace the description with: 'The unit's speed figure divided by the speed reference's figure in the games registry, rounded to two decimals; the validator bands the stored, rounded value. Divide only figures on the same scale: both from the game's own data (unitless game values, such as the Command & Conquer Wiki's land speed, count), or both in real units (convert km/h and m/s). A number whose scale the source does not explain, or that is on a different scale from the reference's figure, does not count. Record it whenever such a figure exists, the reference unit itself included (1). For a series game, take the figure as the Series games convention says, and name the title and model in mobility.notes. With no usable figure, leave it out, set the band from words (see Speed bands) and add an uncertain entry for mobility/speed. Stored only so the band can be recomputed; the generator and app never show or use it.'

(2) 'On the ground it normally fights on' can be read as creep for Zerg, who fight on creep. The r5 note says base speed with no creep.

(5) Aircraft are not covered by the land and water wording.

Speed test: Dunne 0.69 very slow. It also matches the registry note examples: RA2 Rhino 1.5 medium, RA2 IFV and Drone 2.5 fast, Generals Crusader 1.5 medium, Iron Harvest Rycerz 0.7 slow. The pilot edges work: 15 s gives medium and 11 s gives short. I verified the Battlefield figures on C's downloaded pages. Flares: about 11 s in BF3; 'up to 15 seconds' in BF4, after which an update 'reduced reload time' without giving a new figure. ECM: 10 s, counted from activation. Extinguisher: 25 s, cut to 4 s by a late BF4 patch.
Five problems:
(1) The flares are not 'short either way'. Under exact edges BF4's 15 s is medium, so a coder who takes BF4's pre-update figure gets medium and one who falls back to BF3 gets short. This needs the superseded-figure rule (series revision) and a rule for spans such as 'up to 15'.
(2) 'Leave it out when no source gives a figure' contradicts the unchanged per-life term. A one-use-per-life ability has no figure, so one coder leaves it out and another picks per-life.
(3) Exact edges make game speed matter. SC2 values in Normal game seconds are 1.4 times the Faster (real) values, so a 20 s Normal cooldown is 14.3 real seconds: medium against short.
(4) Abilities with charges have no rule.
(5) 'Put the switch time in the summary' invites seconds, against the no-figures convention.
Cross-group flag kept: requiring the mechanic page collides with the three-source cap.

verdicts.revised_change:
List description: 'How often an ability can be used: the wait from one use until it can be used again. Band the source's cooldown figure alone; do not add the time the effect lasts. Use real seconds at the game's normal multiplayer speed (StarCraft II: Faster). Where the source gives a span ("8 to 12 seconds", "up to 15 seconds"), band its largest value. For an ability with charges, band the time to regain one charge. Edges are exact, and a value on an edge takes the higher band. An ability that comes back only at a resupply point or on respawn is per-life, with or without a figure. An ability with no wait has no band: leave cooldown out. That covers instant orders such as unloading, and mode switches that only take time to finish; say in the summary, in words, how long the switch takes. An ability held back only by a stock, such as Company of Heroes munitions or the unit's energy, has no band unless the source also gives a cooldown.'

short: 'From 5 up to but not including 15 seconds; a couple of uses per fight.'
